narration.text: What if the ordinary life you've built could disappear overnight? How do you live with the fear of losing everything, when you've done nothing wrong? And what does it mean to keep building a life, knowing that everything could still be taken away? We spend much of our lives building things. A career. A home. A family. Some savings. Plans for what we might do when we are older. And if we are fortunate, little by little, life begins to feel stable. For most of my life, that fear has been somewhere in the background. Not always present in my thoughts. But never entirely gone.

I grew up in a place where the possibility of war was never entirely abstract. When I was young, there were moments when that possibility suddenly felt very real. I remember being afraid. I had not yet done my military service, and war meant something very simple to me: What if I have to go? That was about thirty years ago. The war never came. I finished my military service. I worked. I got married. I became a father. Eventually, I got used to living with the possibility. Whenever it felt a little closer, I could only look for reassurance in the arguments around me. They wouldn't really do it. The cost would be too high. It wouldn't make sense. Maybe those arguments are right. I hope they are. But either way, I need something that lets me put the fear aside and get on with my life. Because there is not much else I can do.

I thought getting older would make me less afraid. Instead, the fear changed. When I was young, war threatened a life that had barely begun. Now it threatens a life that took decades to build. A house can be replaced. Money can, at least in theory, be earned again. A job can be found again. But the years it took to build those things are gone forever. At my age, starting over does not feel like an adventure. I don't know if I have another thirty years to build the same life again.

And then I look at Ukraine. What I find hardest to imagine is not only the moment when war begins. It is everything that comes after. How do you live like that for years? Children still grow older. People still need food. Parents still need care. People still work, get sick, celebrate birthdays, and wonder what next year will look like. At some point, war is no longer an emergency. It becomes the condition under which ordinary life has to continue. That is what frightens me. Not only that I might die. That I might live. And have to figure out how to live after the life I spent decades building is gone.

Sometimes I wonder what goes through the minds of people who start wars. Why isn't it enough to take care of your own country? Why must someone else's home become part of your ambition? I know there are answers. History. Territory. Security. Power. National interest. But none of those words changes the question I keep coming back to: Why should my family pay the price for a decision we had nothing to do with? Maybe that is why I feel so helpless. There are many things in life I cannot control. But usually, I can at least do something. I can work harder. I can save more. I can prepare. But I cannot work hard enough to make war impossible.

Sometimes this fear feels a little like thinking about death. Not because war is inevitable. It isn't. But both remind me how little of the future I truly control. There is, however, an important difference. Death ends the planning. War may destroy the plan and leave you here to make another one. So what am I supposed to do? Nothing. At least, nothing that can make the possibility go away. So I go to work. I take care of my family. I save money. I make plans. I keep building. Not because I have solved the fear. I haven't. Part of me still wonders whether one day it will happen. I just don't know when.

And if I reach eighty and it never does? I don't think I will say I worried for nothing. I think I will say: How fortunate I was. I was allowed to have an ordinary life. I worked. I raised a family. I grew old. I made plans for tomorrow, and most mornings, tomorrow arrived looking more or less like the day before. But even then, there would be another question. What about my child? And what about his children? If the danger I worried about when I was young is still there when I am old, then perhaps I did not escape the question. I simply lived long enough to see another generation inherit it. I don't need history to remember my generation as brave. I don't want to find out whether I would be brave. And I don't want my child to have to find out either.

If I am fortunate enough to grow old in peace, I hope that fortune does not end with me. I hope my children can work, build homes, raise families, complain about small things, worry about retirement, and make plans for years that have not arrived yet. I hope they can take tomorrow for granted. To make plans. To build things. To assume there will be time to enjoy them. Maybe that is all I really want. An ordinary life. Not only for me. For them, too.
